positions.commentary: The speaker maintains a positive view on Wells Fargo, noting that the scope of direct damage from the scandal was manageable given the bank's size and that competitors have worse behavioral deficiencies.
The speaker mentions Bank of America as a competitor that had far greater economic consequences to their conduct compared to Wells Fargo.
The speaker mentions that Warren Buffett prefers not to own Coca-Cola internationally, but the speaker actually prefers to own those companies internationally.
The speaker mentions that Heineken and Unilever dropped 20% in the last quarter as a result of the election and the reaction through the Trump bump to go into the U.S.
The speaker mentions that the manager of portfolios has to have the capacity to suffer, and that living through periods of pain is different from just telling investors to do so.
The speaker states that they have almost 13% holding in Berkshire Hathaway and love all those exposures, though they may not find their way to directly own those businesses.

notes: Tom Russo is the Managing Member of Gardner Russo & Gardner, where he manages $11 billion in a long only, global value strategy. Tom buys the stock of global consumer businesses with great brands and holds them for a really long time. He looks for businesses with a capacity to reinvest free cash flow and a capacity to suffer through short-term pain in order to achieve long-term gain. Tom started his investment career at the Sequoia Fund in New York, where he worked from 1984 to 1988. His first partnership, Semper Vic Partners, has compounded at 14.6% per year for 33 years, besting the S&P 500 by 3.6% per annum. Tom is a graduate of Dartmouth College (B.A., 1977), and Stanford Business and Law Schools (JD/MBA, 1984). He has served on Dean's Advisory Council for Stanford Law School, Dartmouth College's President's Leadership Council, and the Advisory Board for the Heilbrunn Center for Graham & Dodd Investing at Columbia Business School, as well as on the boards of the Winston Churchill Foundation of the U.S., Facing History and Ourselves, and Storm King Art Center. Our conversation covers how Tom created an investment strategy by personalizing early lessons from Warren Buffett, the capacity to re-invest, the capacity to suffer, and what it takes to own a stock for decades. Tom's time horizon and fortitude as an investor parallels those of institutions with permanent capital.
